A.explanation: Voltmeter is across fixed plus variable resistor, so $V = I(R_{fixed}+R_{var})$. Since $R_{var}$ is changed, $V$ is not proportional to $I$.

B.explanation: Voltmeter is across the fixed resistor only, so $V = IR_{fixed}$ with constant $R_{fixed}$. Hence $V$ is directly proportional to the series current through the motor.

C.explanation: Voltmeter is across the variable resistor only, so $V = IR_{var}$. Since $R_{var}$ is changed to control speed, $V$ is not proportional to $I$.

D.explanation: Voltmeter is across the supply, so it reads the supply p.d. which stays approximately constant while the motor current is changed.

hints: Notice which two points the voltmeter is connected across in each diagram - fixed resistor, variable resistor, both, or supply.
Recall that for a resistor $V = IR$, so $V$ is proportional to $I$ only if $R$ stays constant while $I$ changes.
Check which circuit puts the voltmeter across a component whose resistance does not change when the motor speed is adjusted.
walkthrough: All components - fixed resistor, variable resistor and motor M - are in one series loop, so the same current $I$ flows through the motor and through both resistors.
For any resistor, the p.d. across it is $V = IR$. Proportionality $V$ proportional to $I$ needs $R$ to be constant.
In A the voltmeter spans both resistors, so $V = I(R_{fixed}+R_{var})$. In C it spans the variable resistor, so $V = IR_{var}$. Both include $R_{var}$ which is altered.
In D the voltmeter spans the supply terminals, so it reads the supply voltage, not a voltage that follows the motor current.
In B the voltmeter spans only the fixed resistor, so $V = IR_{fixed}$ with $R_{fixed}$ constant. As $I$ is gradually changed, $V$ changes in direct proportion. This is option B.
